title: Pas de Cécile, pas de Paris  (No Cécile, No Paris)

segments.t: Back at the agency, Gabriel begged Andréa to talk to Cécile, and she told him to give Cécile some space until tomorrow. That evening Hervé took him to a bar and pointed out the women around them, but Gabriel was not in the mood at all. Meanwhile, Mathias is back in the elegant tea room with Miranda Jones, Tarantino's producer. She has a new worry: she wants to shoot the film in Paris, and for that she needs permits. Mathias sees his chance. You'll hear it all in French first; don't worry if some words slip past you.
Mathias, je veux tourner à Paris.
Paris? C'est une très bonne idée.
Oui, mais il faut des autorisations. Ah, la paperasse française!
C'est plus simple quand on connaît les bonnes personnes.
Vraiment?
Si vous avez besoin d'aide, demandez.
Je connais la ministre de la Culture. C'est une jeune femme brillante.
Et elle adore Cécile de France!
Mais Cécile n'est plus dans le projet.
Je sais. Elle va être très triste.
Alors, tourner à Paris, c'est peut-être impossible.
Elle n'a pas besoin de le savoir.
Elles sont très proches. C'est difficile de cacher des choses à ses amies.
Vous bluffez.
Pas du tout. Pas de Cécile, pas de Paris.
Bon. Je vais parler à Quentin.
Merci, Miranda. Bonne chance!
Let's take it slowly. Miranda opens with what she wants, and the verb she uses is the film-world word for shooting a scene.
Mathias, je veux tourner à Paris.
'Mathias, I want to shoot in Paris.' The first verb means 'I want', and right after it comes a verb in its dictionary form, just like in English. Mathias likes the idea.
Paris? C'est une très bonne idée.
'Paris? That's a very good idea.' The word for 'idea' is feminine, so the little word before it is the feminine 'a'. Then Miranda sighs.
Oui, mais il faut des autorisations.
'Yes, but you need permits.' Here is a really useful expression: those two little words at the start mean 'you need' or 'it takes'. They never change, whoever needs the thing.
Ah, la paperasse française!
'Ah, French paperwork!' The French love to complain about their own forms and stamps. Mathias answers with a smooth smile.
C'est plus simple quand on connaît les bonnes personnes.
'It's simpler when you know the right people.' The word in the middle means 'one' or 'people in general'. It sounds like a hint, and it is one.
Vraiment?
'Really?' Miranda is curious now. One word, rising at the end.
Si vous avez besoin d'aide, demandez.
'If you need help, just ask.' Notice the polite form of 'you' all through this scene: Mathias and Miranda are business partners, so they stay formal. The last word is a polite command, 'ask'.
Je connais la ministre de la Culture.
'I know the Minister of Culture.' The verb means to know a person. And the minister is a woman, so she gets the feminine 'the'.
C'est une jeune femme brillante.
'She's a brilliant young woman.' A short adjective like 'young' goes before the noun; a longer one like 'brilliant' goes after it. Then Mathias plays his card.
Et elle adore Cécile de France!
'And she loves Cécile de France!' The verb is stronger than just 'like': it means 'loves'. Miranda sees the problem coming.
Mais Cécile n'est plus dans le projet.

'But Cécile isn't in the project any more.' Here is our second grammar point. The negative in French wraps around the verb, and when the second half is this word, it means 'no longer', 'not any more'.
Je sais. Elle va être très triste.
'I know. She's going to be very sad.' To talk about the near future, take the verb 'to go' and add an infinitive, exactly like 'going to be' in English.
Alors, tourner à Paris, c'est peut-être impossible.
'So shooting in Paris might be impossible.' The word in the middle means 'maybe', and it's a calm way to make a threat. Miranda tries a way out.
Elle n'a pas besoin de le savoir.
'She doesn't need to know.' The negative wraps around the verb again, this time with the ordinary 'not'. Mathias doesn't let go.
Elles sont très proches.
'They're very close.' The pronoun here is the plural for women, since both are women: the minister and Cécile.
C'est difficile de cacher des choses à ses amies.
'It's hard to hide things from your friends.' Literally 'it is difficult to hide things to one's friends'. Miranda isn't fooled.
Vous bluffez.
'You're bluffing.' The same word as in poker, with the polite form of 'you'. And now the line of the scene.
Pas du tout.
'Not at all.' A very handy reply when someone accuses you of something.
Pas de Cécile, pas de Paris.
'No Cécile, no Paris.' Without a verb, the negative word alone is enough, with a little word linking it to the noun. Short and hard to forget. Miranda gives in.
Bon. Je vais parler à Quentin.
'Fine. I'll talk to Quentin.' The near future again: 'I am going to' plus 'talk'. Quentin is Tarantino, of course.
Merci, Miranda. Bonne chance!
'Thank you, Miranda. Good luck!' Mathias has turned a no into a maybe, and he leaves the table very pleased. Now let's hear the whole conversation once more, from the top.
Mathias, je veux tourner à Paris.
Paris? C'est une très bonne idée.
Oui, mais il faut des autorisations. Ah, la paperasse française!
C'est plus simple quand on connaît les bonnes personnes.
Vraiment?
Si vous avez besoin d'aide, demandez.
Je connais la ministre de la Culture. C'est une jeune femme brillante.
Et elle adore Cécile de France!
Mais Cécile n'est plus dans le projet.
Je sais. Elle va être très triste.
Alors, tourner à Paris, c'est peut-être impossible.
Elle n'a pas besoin de le savoir.
Elles sont très proches. C'est difficile de cacher des choses à ses amies.
Vous bluffez.
Pas du tout. Pas de Cécile, pas de Paris.
Bon. Je vais parler à Quentin.
Merci, Miranda. Bonne chance!
That's the end of this scene. When you watch it, listen for the short, punchy line about Cécile and Paris; you'll recognise it straight away. See you in the next scene.
Au revoir, Mathias!
